theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: An acrylic nail enhancement is made by mixing which two products?
options: A thick gel and an activator spray
A liquid monomer and a powder polymer
Nail glue and a strip of silk fabric
A base coat and a coloured polish

questions.stem: How does the acrylic mix harden on the nail?
options: It dries as the water in it evaporates
It hardens only when cured under a lamp
It hardens once an activator spray is put on
It sets by a chemical reaction, with no lamp

questions.stem: What is the best way to control monomer vapour and filing dust at the nail desk?
options: Extraction at the desk that draws vapour and dust away
Air freshener sprayed over the desk every half hour
Windows and doors kept shut so the vapour cannot spread
A desk fan that blows the vapour across the client's face

questions.stem: Which gloves are usually best for handling liquid monomer?
options: Cotton gloves, so that the hands stay cool
Thin vinyl food gloves, worn all day long
Nitrile gloves, changed once they are soiled
No gloves, so that you can feel the brush well

questions.stem: Why must MMA (methyl methacrylate) liquid never be used on nails?
options: It sets too slowly and stays soft for a whole week
It is only sold in bright colours, never clear
It harms skin and nails and is very hard to remove
It has no smell, so a spill is never noticed

questions.stem: Liquid monomer has got onto the client's skin. What should you do?
options: Wipe it off at once, then wash with soap and water
Leave it to set hard, then file it off the skin later
Rub more monomer on to thin it and spread it out
Cover it with powder so that it dries off faster

questions.stem: Acid primer is corrosive: it can burn the skin. How should it be applied?
options: Thickly, over the nail and the cuticle
Generously, so it runs to the side walls
Onto the skin around the nail, to help it grip
Sparingly, to the natural nail plate only

questions.stem: Primer has splashed into a client's eye. What is the first thing to do?
options: Rub the eye gently with a clean tissue
Rinse with plenty of clean running water
Put a few drops of cuticle oil in the eye
Cover the eye with a pad and carry on working

questions.stem: Why should the nail desk be set up with everything you need before the client sits down?
options: So the work flows and you do not leave the client part-way
So the client can pick which tools she would like you to use
So the products can warm up on the desk in the sunlight
So that there is no need to clean any tools during the day

questions.stem: Why do you fill in a record card at the consultation?
options: To work out how much to charge her next time
To keep names for sending birthday cards
To show how busy the salon has been this week
To note her health, nail condition and consent

questions.stem: Which nail condition stops an acrylic service on that nail and needs a referral to a doctor?
options: Small white spots on the nail plate
A thick, yellow nail that crumbles
Fine ridges running along the nail
Short nails that are healthy and pink

questions.stem: A client has had red, itchy, swollen skin around her nails since her last acrylic set. What is the likely cause, and what should you do?
options: It is normal: put a new set on straight away
It is dry skin: file the skin smooth first
It may be an allergy: do not apply, and refer her
It is sunburn: apply it and tell her to stay in shade

questions.stem: When should the nail technician and the client clean their hands?
options: Only at the end, once the nails are finished
Only if the hands look dirty or sticky
Only the technician, as the client is a guest
At the start, before any work on the nails

questions.stem: How should a metal cuticle pusher be made ready for the next client?
options: Clean it, then disinfect it as the maker says
Wipe it on a towel and use it straight away
Rinse it under the tap and dry it on your apron
Leave it in the drawer overnight so germs die

questions.stem: Which of these items is used for one client only and then thrown away?
options: A metal cuticle pusher
A glass dappen dish
A wooden orange stick
An acrylic brush with a cap

questions.stem: Why is the shine removed from the natural nail before the acrylic goes on?
options: So that the nail grows faster under it
So that the product grips the nail better
So that the nail is thinner and bends more
So that her own nail colour is hidden

questions.stem: Which file is best for removing the shine from the natural nail?
options: A coarse 80 grit file, pressed down hard
A fine 180–240 grit file, used lightly
A metal file with deep, sharp teeth
An electric file on its highest speed

questions.stem: What does a nail dehydrator do?
options: Softens the cuticle so that it can be cut
Hardens the acrylic once it is on the nail
Adds a light colour to the nail plate
Removes oil and moisture from the nail

questions.stem: How should a nail tip be chosen for each nail?
options: It fits from side wall to side wall without pressing
It is one size smaller, so it grips the nail very tightly
It is wider than the nail, so it covers the skin too
It is the same size for every finger on both hands

questions.stem: How should a nail form be fitted for sculpting?
options: Loosely, with a gap so the product runs under it
Pointing down, so the nail curves downwards
Snug under the free edge, in line with the nail
Over the top of the nail, covering the plate

questions.stem: What is likely to happen if the acrylic bead is too wet (too much liquid)?
options: It may run onto the skin and lift later
It sets at once and is hard to shape
It turns a darker colour and stays shiny
It becomes stronger and needs no filing

questions.stem: What is likely to happen if the bead is too dry (too much powder)?
options: It runs into the cuticle area and floods
It takes much longer than normal to set
It is grainy, with air bubbles, and weak
It turns very clear and glossy when filed

questions.stem: When applying acrylic over a tip, where is the first bead usually placed?
options: On the cuticle, then pushed out to the tip
On the skin at the side wall, then pressed in
Under the tip, right on the underside of the free edge
Near the free edge, then working back to the cuticle

questions.stem: Why is a small gap left between the acrylic and the skin at the cuticle and side walls?
options: So that the nail can breathe through the gap
Product on skin may cause lifting or allergy
So that her real nail colour can be seen
So that the acrylic sets faster at the edges

questions.stem: Where should the apex (the highest, strongest point) of the acrylic nail sit?
options: Right at the very tip, at the end of the free edge
On the cuticle area, at the base of the nail
Along the side walls, close to the skin there
Over the stress area, near the middle of the nail

questions.stem: How should the acrylic brush be cleaned during and after the service?
options: Soak it in acetone so that the bristles stay soft
Wipe it on a lint-free pad; clean it in monomer
Rinse it in hot soapy water and dry it in the sun
Let the product set on it, then pick it off later

questions.stem: Why should the dish that holds the liquid monomer be small and kept covered?
options: To cut the vapour and keep the liquid clean
To keep the liquid warm so that it sets faster
To stop the powder from changing its colour
So the liquid can be poured back into the bottle

questions.stem: What should you do with the monomer left in the dish at the end of the service?
options: Pour it back into the bottle to save money
Pour it down the sink with lots of water
Dispose of it as the maker and the Centre say
Leave it in the open dish for the next client

questions.stem: How should liquid monomer be stored?
options: In a clear jar on a sunny window ledge
Next to the nail lamp so that it stays warm
Closed, labelled, cool and away from heat
Poured into a drink bottle so it is easy to use

questions.stem: Monomer, primer and acetone are flammable. What does this mean in the salon?
options: Keep them away from heat, flames and smoking
They may only be used outdoors in bright sunlight
They must be kept in the fridge with food
They are safe to use beside a lit candle

questions.stem: Why is a simple paper dust mask not enough on its own at the nail desk?
options: It is too hot to wear in the Jamaican heat
It traps dust, but not the monomer vapour
It stops vapour but lets the dust through
It makes the client think that you are ill

questions.stem: On a nail file, what does a low grit number, such as 100, mean?
options: A fine file, used only for buffing to a shine
A file made only for natural nails
A soft file made for use on toenails
A coarse file that takes product off faster

questions.stem: Looking down the nail from the free edge end, what should you check?
options: An even C-curve (arch), the same on both sides
That the cuticles have been cut right away
That the nail is shiny before the oil goes on
That every nail matches the thumb's length

questions.stem: Which is a sign of a well-made acrylic nail?
options: Thick at the cuticle so that it lasts longer
Product touching the side walls, for strength
A ridge where the tip meets the nail, for grip
Thin at the cuticle, with a smooth, even apex

questions.stem: After filing and buffing, what is put on the skin around the nails?
options: Acetone, to clean the skin
More primer, to keep it soft
Cuticle oil, rubbed in well
Monomer, to seal the edges

questions.stem: Which aftercare advice should you give a client with new acrylic nails?
options: Pick off any lifted product as soon as it lifts
Wear gloves to clean and do not use nails as tools
Soak the nails in acetone each week to clean them
Wait three months or more before coming back

questions.stem: About how often does a client usually need an infill (maintenance)?
options: Every 2–3 days
Every 2–3 weeks
Every 6 months or so
Only when a nail falls off

questions.stem: During an infill, what must be done with acrylic that has lifted?
options: Thin and blend it away before new product goes on
Glue it down and put new acrylic over the top
Pull it off with nippers to save time
Leave it there, as the new product will seal it in

questions.stem: Why is lifted acrylic a risk to the natural nail?
options: It makes the natural nail grow too fast
It changes the colour of the polish that is on top
It makes the acrylic set too hard later
Germs and water trapped under it can infect it

questions.stem: Which is a common cause of acrylic lifting near the cuticle?
options: Using a fresh, well-fitted tip for each finger
Washing hands with soap after the service
Oil or dust left on the nail before applying
Placing the apex over the stress area

questions.stem: What is the safe way to remove acrylic nails?
options: Prise them off with a metal cuticle pusher
Pull them off with a pair of cuticle nippers
Soak them in hot water and twist them off
File off the bulk, then soak them in acetone

questions.stem: During soak-off, how should the softened acrylic be taken off?
options: Scrape hard with a metal pusher until bare
File the natural nail hard to get every bit
Gently ease it off with a wooden stick
Peel the soft layers off with your own nails

questions.stem: Why should you protect the skin and keep the area ventilated when using acetone?
options: It dries skin; its vapour can catch fire
It stains the skin a yellow colour for weeks
It makes the natural nails grow too fast
It sets hard on the skin, just like acrylic

questions.stem: During the service, a client says her fingertips are tingling and itching. What should you do?
options: Carry on, but work faster so that you finish sooner
Stop, clean product off the skin, and record it
Tell her this is normal and add more primer
Give her a tablet from the first-aid box

questions.stem: A supplier offers very cheap acrylic liquid in a bottle with no label. What should you do?
options: Refuse it, and buy labelled EMA liquid with a data sheet
Buy it, and test it on your own nails first
Buy it, and mix it half and half with your usual liquid
Buy it, but use it only on clients with strong nails

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

On a pink-and-white acrylic nail, what is the curved line where the pink meets the white called?

What is the name of the folds of skin along each side of the nail?
Which colour of acrylic powder is used for the free edge of a pink-and-white nail?

essays.stem: Explain how you would control monomer vapour and filing dust at the nail desk, to protect yourself and the client.
essays.modelAnswer: I work in a well-ventilated room and use extraction at the desk, set so that it draws vapour and dust down and away from both of our breathing zones. I pour only a small amount of monomer into a small dish with a lid, and I close the bottles straight after use. Waste with product on it goes into a metal bin with a lid, which is emptied at the end of each day. I file carefully with the extraction on, and I brush the dust into the extractor or wipe it up, rather than blowing it into the air. I wear a well-fitted dust mask and safety glasses when filing, but I remember that a dust mask does not stop vapour, so the extraction must still be on. I do not eat or drink at the desk. I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Good room ventilation and extraction at the desk that draws vapour and dust away
Only a little monomer, in a small covered dish; bottles closed after use
Product waste in a metal bin with a lid, emptied daily
Dust mask and safety glasses when filing, knowing a dust mask does not stop vapour
No eating or drinking at the desk; follows the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

essays.stem: Explain how liquid monomer and primer must be handled safely, and why MMA liquid must never be used.
essays.modelAnswer: I use only professional EMA (ethyl methacrylate) liquid from a known supplier, in its labelled bottle, and I read the safety data sheet. I never use MMA liquid. It does not stick well, so the natural nail is often filed thin to make it grip. It sets so hard that a knock can tear the nail away from the nail bed instead of breaking the acrylic. It hardly soaks off in acetone, and it can cause skin allergies and irritation. Primer, especially acid primer, is corrosive. I apply it sparingly to the natural nail plate only, never to the skin, and close the bottle at once. I wear nitrile gloves, keep all product off the client's skin, and keep everything away from heat and flames. If product touches the skin, I wipe it off and wash with soap and water. If it gets in an eye, I rinse with plenty of clean running water and get medical help.
markingPoints: Uses only labelled professional EMA products and reads the safety data sheet
Never MMA: the nail is over-filed, the hard product can tear the nail off, it is hard to remove and causes allergies
Primer applied sparingly to the nail plate only, never on the skin; bottle closed at once
Nitrile gloves; product kept off the skin; away from heat and flames
Skin contact: wipe and wash; eye: rinse with plenty of clean running water and get medical help

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a consultation before an acrylic service, and what you would do if you found a contraindication.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the client and seat her comfortably at a clean desk. I ask about her health, any allergies (especially to nail products), her medicines, her job and hobbies, and the look she wants. I clean my hands and hers, then check her hands and nails in good light. I look for contraindications such as fungal or bacterial infection, swelling, cuts, broken skin, warts, eczema, a separated or bruised nail, or signs of an earlier allergy. I write what I find and what we agree on the record card, and she signs it to give her consent. If there is an infection or an allergy, I do not carry out the service. I explain kindly, without naming a disease, because I cannot diagnose, and I suggest she sees her doctor. A small local problem, such as one bruised nail, may mean leaving that nail out. I keep the card private.
markingPoints: Asks about health, allergies, medicines, lifestyle and the look wanted
Cleans hands and checks the hands and nails in good light
Names likely contraindications (infection, broken skin, swelling, separated nail, earlier allergy)
Records the findings on the record card and gets signed consent
Does not treat an infection or allergy; explains tactfully and refers to a doctor

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you prepare the natural nail before acrylic is applied, and say why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First I clean my hands and the client's hands, and remove any old polish so that I can see the nails clearly. I gently push back the cuticle with a clean pusher and lift off any dead cuticle stuck to the nail plate, because product on cuticle will lift. I shape the free edge short and even with a fine file. I lightly remove the shine from the nail plate with a 180–240 grit file or buffer, so that the product has something to grip. I do not file hard, because a thin nail is weak and sore. I brush away all the dust. I wipe each nail with dehydrator to take away oil and moisture, which also helps to stop lifting. Then I apply primer sparingly to the natural nail only, as the maker says. From then on I ask the client not to touch her face or hair, so that no oil gets back onto the nails.
markingPoints: Hands cleaned and old polish removed
Cuticle gently pushed back and dead tissue removed from the nail plate
Shine lightly removed with a fine file, without over-filing
Dust removed and nail dehydrated to take off oil and moisture
Primer applied sparingly to the nail only, and the nails kept free of oil

essays.stem: Describe the steps for applying nail tips with an acrylic overlay.
essays.modelAnswer: After preparing the nails, I choose a tip for each finger that fits from side wall to side wall. I put a little adhesive in the well, rock the tip on from the free edge at an angle to push out the air, and hold it until it sets. I cut the tip to length and blend its edge into the nail so that there is no ridge, taking care not to file the natural nail. I remove the dust and apply primer if the maker says so. I dip the brush in monomer, wipe off the extra and pick up a bead of the right mix. I place the first bead near the free edge and shape it, then a second over the stress area to form the apex, and a small, thin bead near the cuticle, leaving a tiny gap from the skin. When the product has set, I file and shape it, check the C-curve and thickness from every side, buff it smooth and finish with cuticle oil.
markingPoints: Tip chosen to fit side wall to side wall and applied without air bubbles
Tip cut and blended with no ridge, without filing the natural nail
Bead of the right mix: free edge first, then apex over the stress area, then thin at the cuticle
Small gap left at the cuticle and side walls; no product on the skin
Filed, checked from all sides, buffed and finished with cuticle oil

essays.stem: Compare a tip with an acrylic overlay and a sculpted acrylic nail made on a form. Say when each might be chosen.
essays.modelAnswer: Both give the client a longer, stronger nail made with liquid and powder, and both need the same careful preparation of the natural nail. For a tip and overlay, a plastic tip is glued to the nail to make the extra length, and acrylic is put over the tip and the nail. It is quicker, and the tip gives the shape, so it suits a newer technician and a client with even, regular nails. For a sculpted nail, a form is fitted snugly under the free edge and the whole extension is built in acrylic, with no tip. It takes more skill and time, but the shape and the curve can be made to suit the client exactly. It suits nails that a tip will not fit well, such as very curved or uneven nails, and it is often chosen for a pink-and-white finish with a clear smile line. Both kinds need an infill every 2–3 weeks.
markingPoints: Both are liquid and powder over a prepared nail, and both need infills
Tip and overlay: a glued tip gives the length and shape; quicker and easier
Sculpted: a form is fitted under the free edge and the extension is built in acrylic with no tip
Sculpting takes more skill and time but can be shaped to suit the client
Gives a sensible reason for choosing each (for example, tips do not fit very curved nails)

essays.stem: Describe how to remove acrylic nails safely, and explain why they must never be prised or pulled off.
essays.modelAnswer: I make sure the area is ventilated, wear gloves, and keep the acetone away from heat and flames. I clip the free edge short and file off most of the bulk with a medium file, stopping before I reach the natural nail. I put cuticle oil or a barrier cream on the skin around the nails. I soak the nails in acetone, either in a small dish or with acetone-soaked cotton wrapped in foil, for as long as the maker says. I check them now and then and gently ease the softened product off with a wooden stick. If some is still hard, I soak it again rather than forcing it. Finally, I lightly buff the nails, wash the hands, and apply cuticle oil and hand cream. Prising or pulling acrylic off tears away layers of the natural nail plate. This leaves the nail thin, weak and painful, and it can lift the nail from the bed and let infection in.
markingPoints: Ventilation, gloves, and acetone kept away from heat and flames
Free edge cut short and the bulk filed off without damaging the natural nail
Skin protected; nails soaked in acetone (dish, or cotton and foil) as the maker says
Softened product eased off gently with a wooden stick; soaked again rather than forced
Explains that prising tears the nail plate, leaving it thin and sore and open to infection

essays.stem: Explain how you carry out an infill on acrylic nails that have grown out, including how you deal with lifting.
essays.modelAnswer: I ask the client how the nails have been and check each one for lifting, cracks, discolouration or signs of infection. If there is an infection or an allergy, I stop and refer her to a doctor. I clean our hands, remove any polish and gently push back the cuticle on the new growth. With a file, I carefully thin and blend away any lifted product until it is flush with the nail, because product left lifted traps water and germs. I never nip or pull lifted product off. I reduce the thickness of the old acrylic and rebalance the shape, moving the apex back over the stress area. I remove the shine from the new nail growth only, take away the dust, and dehydrate and prime it. I apply a small bead to the regrowth, blend it into the old product and keep it thin at the cuticle. I file, shape and buff, finish with cuticle oil, and rebook her in about 2–3 weeks.
markingPoints: Checks each nail for lifting, cracks, discolouration and infection
Thins and blends lifted product away; never nips or pulls it
Reduces the bulk and rebalances so that the apex is back over the stress area
Prepares only the new growth (shine off, dehydrate, prime)
Applies thin product to the regrowth, blends and finishes, and rebooks

essays.stem: Explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and describe how you make your nail station and tools ready for the next client.
essays.modelAnswer: Cleaning means removing dirt, dust and product with soap and water or a cleaner. It must be done first, because a disinfectant cannot work through dirt. Disinfecting means using a chemical disinfectant, at the strength and for the time the maker gives, to kill most germs on hard surfaces and tools. Sterilising kills all germs, including spores, for example in an autoclave, and is used where the Centre's rules need it. Between clients I throw away single-use items such as orange sticks, paper files and buffers, and put used towels in the laundry. I wash metal tools such as pushers and nippers in warm soapy water, rinse and dry them, then put them fully into the disinfectant for the time stated, and store them in a clean, closed container. I wipe the desk and bottles with disinfectant, put down a fresh towel, and empty the lidded bin when needed.
markingPoints: Cleaning: removes dirt and product, and is done first
Disinfecting: a chemical at the maker's strength and time, which kills most germs
Sterilising: kills all germs, including spores (for example in an autoclave)
Single-use items thrown away; metal tools cleaned, then disinfected, and stored covered
Desk and bottles wiped down, a fresh towel put out, and the bin emptied

essays.stem: Describe the aftercare advice you would give a client after a new set of acrylic nails, and say why each point matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I tell the client to wear gloves for washing up, cleaning and gardening, because water and chemicals can weaken the bond and dry the skin. She should not use her nails as tools to open cans or scrape things, because this can lift or break them. She should rub cuticle oil into the skin around the nails every day, to keep the skin soft and the nails flexible. If a nail lifts, cracks or comes off, she should not pick it, bite it or glue it herself, because water trapped under lifted product can cause an infection. She should come back to the salon instead. She should return for an infill every 2–3 weeks. If she sees redness, swelling, itching, or green or yellow marks, she should come back at once or see a doctor. When she wants the nails off, she should book a professional removal and never pull them off.
markingPoints: Gloves for wet work and cleaning products
Do not use the nails as tools
Cuticle oil every day
Do not pick or repair lifted nails at home; return to the salon, with infills every 2–3 weeks
Report redness, itching, swelling or discolouration; professional removal only

practical1.title: Nail tips with an acrylic overlay on a partner's nails
practical1.brief: As a group, set up safe nail stations in the Centre's salon, with good ventilation and extraction at each desk. Work in a circle: each member is the nail technician for the next member, who agrees to be the client, so that everyone is both technician and client. Each technician carries out a short consultation, checks for contraindications and fills in a record card that the client signs. The technician then prepares two nails, fits and blends tips, and applies an acrylic overlay to those two nails, shapes and finishes them, and gives aftercare advice. If a member has a contraindication, or does not agree to be a client, the technician works on a practice hand instead. Each member also takes one job for the group: setting up the stations, checking that the extraction is on and the lids are closed, taking the photos, or leading the clean-down. Photograph each stage below, showing only hands and nails, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group, with the record cards.
materials: Nail desks with good lighting and desk extraction (or the extraction the Centre provides)
Professional EMA liquid monomer, acrylic powder (clear or natural) and primer, all in labelled containers
Small dappen dishes with lids, and acrylic brushes
Nail tips in a range of sizes, nail adhesive and tip cutters
Files (100/180 and 180/240 grit), buffers and dust brushes
Cuticle pushers, orange sticks, dehydrator, lint-free pads and cuticle oil
Nitrile gloves, dust masks and safety glasses
Record cards and pens
A metal bin with a lid, disinfectant, paper towels and fresh towels
A practice hand for any member who cannot be a client
Phone or tablet for photos
photos: The nail stations set up, with extraction, covered dishes and the lidded bin
Each member's completed record card, with the client's name covered
The two nails prepared: cuticles pushed back, shine removed and dehydrated
Tips fitted and blended, before the acrylic goes on
The acrylic overlay applied, before filing
The two finished nails, top view and side view
The stations cleaned, tools in disinfectant and waste in the lidded bin
checklist: Carried out a consultation, checked for contraindications and completed the record card with signed consent
Wore nitrile gloves, and a dust mask and safety glasses when filing; kept the extraction on and the lids closed
Prepared the natural nails correctly, without over-filing
Fitted tips from side wall to side wall and blended them with no ridge
Used the right bead mix, kept product off the skin and placed the apex over the stress area
Finished nails: even shape, thin at the cuticle, smooth, with a good C-curve
Cleaned and disinfected the tools and left the station safe and tidy
safety: Keep the extraction on and the room ventilated; keep monomer in a small covered dish and close bottles after use
Never use MMA liquid; use only labelled products and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep primer and monomer off the skin; if any gets in an eye, rinse with plenty of clean running water and get help
Keep all products away from heat and flames, and do not eat or drink at the desk
Do not work on anyone with an infection, broken skin or a known allergy to nail products
Put waste with product on it in the lidded metal bin

practical2.title: Sculpted pink-and-white acrylic nails on forms, and safe soak-off removal
practical2.brief: As a group, set up safe nail stations with good ventilation and desk extraction. Part 1: each member fits nail forms and sculpts two pink-and-white acrylic nails on a practice hand, with white product at the free edge, a clear, even smile line and pink over the nail bed. File, shape and buff both nails to a length and shape the group agrees with the assessor. Members then check each other's nails from the top, the side and the end, and write one strength and one point to improve on a check sheet. Part 2: each member safely removes acrylic from two nails of the next member in the circle, who agrees to it (the nails from Practical 1, or tips with acrylic fixed to a practice hand if there are none), using the file-and-soak method. Finish with cuticle oil and hand cream, and give aftercare advice. Each member also takes one job for the group: setting up, safety checks on the extraction, lids and bin, taking the photos, or leading the clean-down. Photograph each stage below, showing only hands and nails, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group, with the check sheets.
materials: Nail desks with good lighting and desk extraction
Practice hands or practice fingers that take acrylic
Nail forms
Professional EMA liquid monomer, white and pink acrylic powders, and primer, in labelled containers
Small dappen dishes with lids, and acrylic brushes
Files (100/180 and 180/240 grit), buffers and dust brushes
Acetone, cotton pads, foil wraps or a small soak bowl, and wooden orange sticks
Cuticle oil, hand cream and barrier cream

checklist: Set up a safe station: extraction on, small covered dish, lids closed, PPE worn
Fitted the forms snugly under the free edge and in line with the nail
Placed white product with a clear, even smile line and pink over the nail bed
Built a balanced nail: apex over the stress area, thin at the cuticle, even C-curve
Filed and buffed to the agreed shape, with smooth, even edges
Removed acrylic safely: bulk filed, skin protected, soaked, eased off gently and never prised
Finished with cuticle oil and gave aftercare advice after the removal
Cleaned and disinfected the tools and left the station safe and tidy
safety: Keep the extraction on and the room ventilated; keep monomer in a small covered dish and close bottles after use
Never use MMA liquid; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Acetone and monomer are flammable: keep them away from heat and flames
Wear nitrile gloves, and a dust mask and safety glasses when filing
Never prise, pull or nip acrylic off the natural nail
Put waste with product or acetone on it in the lidded metal bin
